label: Alcohol control (shared figures for every model that values heavy drinking averted)

source.title: IHME, Global Burden of Disease 2023, deaths by risk factor, via Our World in Data
source.page: High alcohol use deaths column, Liberia, 2023

rows.explainer: All deaths GBD attributes to alcohol use in Liberia: the burden a Liberian alcohol tax works on (charityevals' Concentric Policies model). Turned into DALYs with death_ages.alcohol_deaths_per_daly_west_africa.

rows.label: Fall in alcohol's burden per 1% rise in alcohol prices (share of a percent)

source.title: Wagenaar, Salois and Komro, Effects of beverage alcohol price and tax levels on drinking: a meta-analysis of 1003 estimates from 112 studies, Addiction 2009
source.quote: Price/tax also affects heavy drinking significantly (mean reported elasticity = -0.28, individual-level r = -0.01, P < 0.01), but the magnitude of effect is smaller than effects on overall drinking.

rows.explainer: Alcohol's harm comes mostly from heavy drinking, whose mean reported price elasticity is -0.28 (overall drinking falls more: -0.46 for beer, -0.69 for wine, -0.80 for spirits, the same meta-analysis). So 1% higher prices cut the burden about 0.28%. Range 0.1 (heavy drinkers responding least, as the meta-analysis finds them less responsive than drinkers overall) to 0.5 (the burden following overall drinking). Drinking that carries no tax (unrecorded alcohol) is each model's enforcement row, not here.

rows.label: Years from less heavy drinking until the health gain
rows.explainer: Our judgment: injuries, violence and alcohol's part in tuberculosis fall within the year; cirrhosis and cancers over a decade or more. 3 years, from 0.5 to 8. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Harm of alcohol to people other than the drinker, as a share of the drinker's own burden
rows.explainer: Our judgment: GBD counts the drinker's own burden (its road-injury deaths include some others killed by drink-drivers); violence, neglect, fetal alcohol harm and others' injuries fall outside it. No quantified estimate for poor countries was found (surveys of harm to others come from rich countries and count harms, not DALYs), so a modest share: 10%, from 0 to 30%. Read as a side effect of heavy drinking averted.

source.title: WHO Global Health Observatory, indicators SA_0000001747 and SA_0000001821

rows.explainer: Recorded over recorded plus unrecorded drinking: 0.545 / 1.682 = 32%. WHO's own intervals are wide (recorded 0.2 to 0.9 litres, unrecorded 0.4 to 1.9), so 20% to 50%. Only this share carries a change in excise.
